text: Habits are not bad. <break time="0.8s" /> We need them. <break time="0.8s" /> To survive. <break time="0.8s" /> Understanding how the brain uses habits. <break time="0.8s" /> And how you can work with them. <break time="0.8s" /> Is essential for business. <break time="0.8s" /> One question to ask is. <break time="0.8s" /> Are you really trying to break a habit. <break time="0.8s" /> Or would you do better. <break time="0.8s" /> By attaching to another one. <break time="0.8s" /> Known as temptation bundling. <break time="0.8s" /> Wharton professor Katy Milkman led. <break time="0.8s" /> A research project called Holding the Hunger Games Hostage at the Gym. <break time="0.8s" /> Where participants could only have access to their audio devices. <break time="0.8s" /> While at the gym. <break time="0.8s" /> This uses a tempting habit. <break time="0.8s" /> , listening to that awesome audiobook. <break time="0.8s" /> And combines it with a habit people would like to build. <break time="0.8s" /> But may otherwise feel forced to put off. <break time="0.8s" /> Like exercising. <break time="0.8s" /> The participants whose devices were held hostage. <break time="0.8s" /> Were 51 percent more likely to visit the gym. <break time="0.8s" /> And the really amazing thing. <break time="0.8s" /> Is what happened after it was over. <break time="0.8s" /> Nearly two thirds opted to pay. <break time="0.8s" /> To have gym only access for their devices.
